fields.Front: What five core classes typically make up a meeting scheduler system?
fields.Back: Meeting, Room, User/Participant, Calendar, and TimeSlot (Interval) — Meeting ties a TimeSlot to a Room and a set of Participants; Calendar aggregates a User's Meetings.

fields.Front: What is the responsibility of the TimeSlot (Interval) class?
fields.Back: Holds a start and end timestamp and exposes an overlaps(other) method — the core reusable building block for all conflict-detection logic (room booking, participant double-booking, free-slot search).

fields.Front: Why is the interval-overlap check typically written with strict '<' rather than '<=' at the boundaries?
fields.Back: So a meeting ending exactly when another starts (e.g. 10:00-11:00 and 11:00-12:00) is NOT treated as a conflict — using '<=' would incorrectly flag back-to-back, non-overlapping meetings as conflicting.

fields.Front: What enum models how a Meeting repeats, and what values does it hold?
fields.Back: RecurrenceType: NONE, DAILY, WEEKLY, MONTHLY (sometimes CUSTOM with an explicit rule).

fields.Front: What is the core algorithmic technique for detecting a room double-booking against N existing bookings efficiently, rather than a full O(n) linear scan each time?
fields.Back: Keep each Room's bookings in a sorted structure ordered by start time (e.g. a TreeMap/balanced BST or interval tree); to check a new [start, end), look up the closest existing bookings around start and only compare against those neighbors — O(log n) instead of O(n).

fields.Front: What data structure gives true O(log n) overlap queries for arbitrary insert/delete of many intervals, and why is it better than a simple sorted list for a busy scheduler?
fields.Back: An interval tree (each node stores an interval plus the max endpoint in its subtree) — unlike a sorted-by-start list, it supports efficient overlap queries even when intervals have very different lengths, without scanning past every interval that starts before the query but ends after it starts.

fields.Front: Which design fits expanding a recurring Meeting (WEEKLY, ends after N occurrences) into concrete Meeting instances, and why?
fields.Back: Strategy pattern for recurrence expansion: each RecurrenceType (DAILY/WEEKLY/MONTHLY) implements a common RecurrenceStrategy.nextOccurrences(start, rule) interface, so SchedulerService doesn't need type-specific branching to generate instances.

fields.Front: Why can't a recurring Meeting simply be stored as N separate Meeting rows generated once and forgotten?
fields.Back: Individual occurrences can be modified independently (one instance moved, cancelled, or renamed without affecting the series) — the classic 'edit this event / this and following / all events' problem, requiring either exception records per-instance or storing the recurrence rule and materializing occurrences on read with an override list.

fields.Front: What edge case makes finding a common free slot among N participants harder than checking one person's calendar?
fields.Back: You must intersect the free time of ALL participants — a slot is only valid if it doesn't overlap ANY participant's existing meetings, so the algorithm merges each participant's busy intervals, then finds gaps common to every participant's free-time list (an intersection of free intervals, not a union).

fields.Front: Why must all Meeting start/end times be normalized to a single reference (e.g. stored in UTC) rather than each participant's local time?
fields.Back: Participants may be in different timezones; comparing raw local times without a common reference would misclassify overlaps/conflicts. Store timestamps in UTC internally and convert to each participant's local timezone only for display.

fields.Front: Should a User be allowed to be double-booked (two overlapping meetings on their own calendar), and how should the design decide?
fields.Back: It's a policy decision, not purely technical: tentative meetings may be allowed to overlap so the user can choose later, but the SchedulerService should expose the conflict via hasConflict(user, timeslot) so the caller (UI) can warn or block, rather than silently allowing or silently rejecting.

fields.Front: What API method would a client call to schedule a new meeting, and what should it check before creating it?
fields.Back: scheduleMeeting(User organizer, List<User> participants, Room room, TimeSlot slot) — must check the Room isn't already booked for an overlapping slot AND that no required participant already has a conflicting Meeting (or degrade gracefully to a warning for optional attendees).

fields.Front: What API method finds open slots for a group, and what parameters does it need?
fields.Back: findAvailableSlots(List<User> participants, Duration duration, DateRange searchWindow) — returns a list of TimeSlots of at least duration where every participant is free within searchWindow.

fields.Front: When cancelling one occurrence of a recurring Meeting, what should the system NOT do?
fields.Back: It should not cancel the entire recurring series — it must create/mark an exception for just that single occurrence, leaving the rest of the recurrence rule and its future/past instances untouched.

fields.Front: Java: implement a TimeSlot.overlaps(other) method using the strict-inequality interval overlap check.
fields.Back:
import java.time.LocalDateTime;

class TimeSlot {
    private final LocalDateTime start;
    private final LocalDateTime end;

    public TimeSlot(LocalDateTime start, LocalDateTime end) {
        this.start = start;
        this.end = end;
    }

    public LocalDateTime getStart() { return start; }
    public LocalDateTime getEnd() { return end; }

    public boolean overlaps(TimeSlot other) {
        return this.start.isBefore(other.end) && other.start.isBefore(this.end);
    }
}

fields.Front: Python: write find_free_slots(busy_intervals, window_start, window_end, min_duration) that returns gaps of at least min_duration between sorted busy intervals.
fields.Back:
def find_free_slots(busy_intervals, window_start, window_end, min_duration):
    intervals = sorted(busy_intervals)
    free_slots = []
    cursor = window_start

    for start, end in intervals:
        if start > cursor and (start - cursor) >= min_duration:
            free_slots.append((cursor, start))
        cursor = max(cursor, end)

    if window_end > cursor and (window_end - cursor) >= min_duration:
        free_slots.append((cursor, window_end))

    return free_slots

fields.Front: Java: implement a Room class backed by a TreeMap of bookings that checks only its nearest neighbors for an overlap in isAvailable(requested).
fields.Back:
import java.time.LocalDateTime;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.TreeMap;

class Room {
    private final TreeMap<LocalDateTime, TimeSlot> bookingsByStart = new TreeMap<>();

    public boolean isAvailable(TimeSlot requested) {
        Map.Entry<LocalDateTime, TimeSlot> before = bookingsByStart.floorEntry(requested.getStart());
        Map.Entry<LocalDateTime, TimeSlot> after = bookingsByStart.ceilingEntry(requested.getStart());

        if (before != null && before.getValue().overlaps(requested)) return false;
        if (after != null && after.getValue().overlaps(requested)) return false;
        return true;
    }

    public void book(TimeSlot slot) {
        bookingsByStart.put(slot.getStart(), slot);
    }
}

fields.Front: Python: write expand_weekly(first_start, first_end, occurrences) that generates the (start, end) tuples for a weekly recurring meeting.
fields.Back:
from datetime import timedelta

def expand_weekly(first_start, first_end, occurrences):
    meetings = []
    for i in range(occurrences):
        offset = timedelta(weeks=i)
        meetings.append((first_start + offset, first_end + offset))
    return meetings
